meta.title: Ancient Civilizations
meta.subtitle: Egypt, Mesopotamia, Anatolia and the Aegean, c. 3500–539 BCE
meta.description: Bronze Age and early Iron Age civilizations of the eastern Mediterranean and the Near East, from early Sumer to Cyrus taking Babylon.
meta.credits: Dates and events come from English Wikipedia (read 17 November 2026) and the scholarly works it cites; each event lists its sources. Ancient dates are uncertain and scholars disagree. Faded bar ends and whiskers show the spread of dates the cited sources give, and the chronology menus re-plot a region under another dating system. Compiled with AI assistance and not yet reviewed by a specialist.

middle.name: Middle Chronology
middle.description: Fall of Babylon in 1595 BCE; Hammurabi reigns 1792–1750 BCE. Wikipedia calls it the most commonly seen solution, 'but there is far from a consensus'.

source.sourceLocation: Middle Bronze Age; table 'Variant Middle Bronze Age chronologies'

high.name: High (Long) Chronology
high.description: Fall of Babylon in 1651 BCE: 56 years earlier than the Middle Chronology. Applied here to dates before 1400 BCE (see docs/ancient-sources.md).

low.name: Low (Short) Chronology
low.description: Fall of Babylon in 1531 BCE: 64 years later than the Middle Chronology. Where a source gives its own short-chronology date, that date is used instead of the shift.

aegean-high.description: Absolute dates for the Minoan and Helladic phases based on radiocarbon (Manning 2012), with the Thera eruption in the late 17th or 16th century BCE.

aegean-low.name: Low (conventional) Aegean chronology
aegean-low.description: Dates from archaeological synchronisms with Egypt, roughly a century later for the eruption and early Late Bronze Age phases.

events.title: Urukean expansion
events.descr: The peak of Uruk's influence in the Late Uruk phase: colonies and trading posts far beyond southern Mesopotamia, monumental building and administrative record-keeping.

sources.sourceLocation: Outline of the 4th millennium BC in the Near East

events.title: Earliest proto-cuneiform tablets (Uruk IV)
events.descr: Administrative tablets from Uruk's Eanna district, the earliest stage of the writing that became cuneiform. Dates are the CDLI's, as cited by Wikipedia.

sources.sourceLocation: Outline of the 4th millennium BC (CDLI, Uruk IV)

events.title: Royal tombs of Ur
events.descr: The richly furnished royal burials of Ur, including the Standard of Ur, belong to Early Dynastic IIIa.

events.title: Lugal-zage-si unites Sumer
events.descr: King of Umma, then of Uruk. He ended Umma's long border war with Lagash and ruled Ur, Nippur, Larsa and Kish: the last Sumerian king before Akkadian rule. The reign dates are from the article's navbox and carry no footnote.

sources.sourceLocation: Reign; navbox '3rd dynasty of Uruk, 2358–2334 BC'

events.title: Reign of Sargon of Akkad
events.descr: Founder of the Akkadian Empire, often called the first empire. Within the middle chronology, scholars offer several reign dates; all are recorded here.

events.title: Sargon conquers Sumer
events.descr: Sargon defeats Lugal-zage-si, takes Uruk and brings the Sumerian cities under Akkad; later campaigns reach Elam and Mari.

events.title: Reign of Naram-Sin
events.descr: Sargon's grandson. He took the title 'King of the Four Corners', was the first Mesopotamian king to claim divinity in his lifetime, and campaigned as far as Anatolia and Ebla.

events.title: Fall of Akkad and Gutian rule
events.descr: After weak successors, Akkadian rule ends and Gutian kings based at Adab hold sway in Sumer.

events.title: Utu-hengal of Uruk defeats the Gutians
events.descr: Utu-hengal defeats the Gutian king Tirigan and restores Sumerian kingship, only to be ousted by Ur-Nammu about eight years later.

source.sourceLocation: end of Gutian rule, c. 2119 BC

startDates.note: The page gives both dates without naming a chronology; the later one matches the low chronology.

events.title: Ur-Nammu founds the Third Dynasty of Ur
events.descr: Ur-Nammu takes the titles King of Ur and King of Sumer and Akkad. The Code of Ur-Nammu, the oldest surviving law code, is attributed to him (Wikipedia gives it no date).

events.title: Reign of Shulgi
events.descr: Ur-Nammu's son reigns for about half the dynasty's length, consolidating the kingdom into an empire on the Akkadian model.

events.title: Elamites destroy Ur
events.descr: A coalition from Anshan and Shimashki deals the final blow to the Third Dynasty of Ur under Ibbi-Sin; Ur is destroyed. Isin and Larsa rise in its place.

source.sourceLocation: lead (low chronology end of Ur III)

events.title: Sumu-abum makes Babylon independent
events.descr: The Amorite chieftain Sumu-abum founds the First Dynasty of Babylon.

events.title: Reign of Hammurabi
events.descr: The sixth king of Babylon reigns 43 years, conquers Larsa, Eshnunna and Mari, and issues his law code. His reign is the usual reference point for the competing chronologies.

events.title: Hammurabi conquers Larsa
events.descr: Babylon defeats Rim-Sin I of Larsa in Hammurabi's 30th year, gaining Nippur, Ur, Uruk and Isin and ending the Isin–Larsa period.

events.title: Hammurabi takes Eshnunna and Mari
events.descr: Eshnunna falls in 1762 and Mari in 1761; Mari's palace is burned, preserving its great archive (1774–1761 BCE).

events.title: Code of Hammurabi
events.descr: The basalt stele of nearly 300 laws, compiled late in Hammurabi's reign. It was later carried off to Susa as plunder, where it was found in 1901.

events.title: Assyrian merchant colony at Kanesh (kārum level II)
events.descr: Old Assyrian merchants trade tin and textiles from a quarter outside the Anatolian city of Kanesh, leaving thousands of tablets. The level ends in a fire.

sources.sourceLocation: Archaeology ('Mesopotamian middle chronology according to Veenhof')

events.title: Trade revives at Kanesh (kārum level Ib)
events.descr: Trade is rebuilt, under the control of Ishme-Dagan I of Assyria, until the colony burns again.

events.title: Reign of Anitta of Kussara
events.descr: Anitta takes Neša (Kanesh) after his father Pithana, defeats Zalpuwa, sacks Hattusa and makes Neša his capital. His inscription is among the oldest texts in Hittite.

events.title: Anitta burns Hattusa
events.descr: A burnt layer at Hattusa is credited to Anitta, who cursed anyone who would resettle the site. The Hittite kings later made it their capital.

events.title: Reign of Ḫattušili I; the capital moves to Hattusa
events.descr: The earliest Hittite king with contemporary records takes the name 'the man of Hattusa', moves his capital there and campaigns into Syria.

source.sourceLocation: p. 25 (via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings)
p. 25 (via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings)

events.title: Alalakh's Level VII palace destroyed
events.descr: Dated by the excavator to the second year of Ḫattušili I's reign, during his Syrian campaigns.

events.title: Reign of Mursili I
events.descr: Ḫattušili's grandson renews the Syrian wars, takes Aleppo and raids Babylon. He is assassinated on his return by a conspiracy led by Ḫantili I and Zidanta I.

source.sourceLocation: p. 25 (via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings)
p. 25 (via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings)

events.title: Mursili I takes Aleppo
events.descr: The Hittites conquer Yamhad and its capital Aleppo before marching about 2,000 km down the Euphrates to Babylon.

events.title: Hittite sack of Babylon
events.descr: Mursili I raids Babylon and ends the dynasty of Hammurabi. The raid wasn't meant to hold territory; the Kassites take control afterwards. This date anchors the competing Mesopotamian chronologies.

events.title: Kassites take power in Babylonia
events.descr: A people from the Zagros mountains take Babylonia after the Hittite raid and rule it for over four centuries.

events.title: Telepinu Proclamation
events.descr: King Telepinu's edict sets rules for the royal succession after generations of murders. Little more than the names of his successors is known for about 80 years.

events.title: Kirta, first king of Mitanni
events.descr: The Hurrian kingdom of Mitanni rises in northern Syria and south-eastern Anatolia, between the Hittites, Egypt, the Kassites and Assyria.

events.title: Reign of Šuppiluliuma I
events.descr: The Hittite empire's great expansion: Mitanni is broken in the One-Year and Six-Year wars, Carchemish is taken, and Hatti becomes a great power that writes to Egypt in the Amarna letters.

source.sourceLocation: via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings (Bryce column)
via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings
via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings

events.title: Ashur-uballit I of Assyria takes Mitanni lands
events.descr: Assyria breaks free of Mitanni and, in the middle of the 14th century, annexes Mitanni territory. Wikipedia notes the Assyrian King List is considered roughly correct from his reign on.

events.title: Reign of Muwatalli II
events.descr: Muwatalli moves the royal seat south to Tarḫuntašša and faces Ramesses II at Kadesh.

sources.sourceLocation: lead (Van De Mieroop 2007, p. 159); Move to Tarhuntassa

source.sourceLocation: via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings

events.title: Battle of Kadesh
events.descr: Ramesses II and Muwatalli II fight on the Orontes in Ramesses's fifth year; both claim victory and the result is a stalemate. Possibly the largest chariot battle ever fought.

startDates.note: 'the high chronology has the date about 20 years earlier'

events.title: Reign of Ḫattušili III
events.descr: Muwatalli's brother, the Hittite commander at Kadesh, deposes his nephew Mursili III (Urhi-Teshub) and makes peace with Egypt.

events.title: Egyptian–Hittite peace treaty
events.descr: Ramesses II and Ḫattušili III agree the earliest surviving peace treaty, about fifteen years after Kadesh. Egyptian and Hittite versions both survive.

source.sourceLocation: body ('the 21st year of Ramesses II's reign (1258 BC)')

events.title: Ramesses II marries a daughter of Ḫattušili III
events.descr: A diplomatic marriage in Ramesses's 34th year seals the peace.

events.title: Reign of Tudḫaliya IV
events.descr: Ḫattušili's son loses to Assyria at Nihriya and claims a conquest of Alashiya (Cyprus).

source.sourceLocation: via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings
via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings

events.title: Battle of Nihriya
events.descr: Tukulti-Ninurta I of Assyria defeats Tudḫaliya IV over the remnants of Mitanni: the first direct defeat of the Hittites by Assyria.

events.title: Assyria annexes what is left of Mitanni (Ḫanigalbat)
events.descr: Under Shalmaneser I the rump Mitanni state, long passed between Hittite and Assyrian control, is finally annexed. The year isn't known; the bar spans his reign.

events.title: Reign of Šuppiluliuma II, last Hittite great king
events.descr: He campaigns against Tarḫuntašša and wins what is described as the first recorded naval battle, off Cyprus. He probably left Hattusa; the old story that he died in its sack is now doubted.

events.title: Hattusa abandoned and burned
events.descr: The Hittite capital is abandoned over several decades; the final fire probably came after the court had left. A severe drought is one suspected cause.

events.title: Neo-Hittite (Syro-Hittite) states
events.descr: Luwian and Aramean successor kingdoms such as Carchemish keep Hittite traditions alive in south-eastern Anatolia and Syria until Assyria absorbs them; Carchemish falls in 717 BCE.

sources.sourceLocation: Late Bronze Age – Early Iron Age transition ('12th century BCE')

source.sourceLocation: infobox (end of Hattusa, after which the states arose)

events.title: Troy VI destroyed
events.descr: The final sublayer of the great Middle–Late Bronze Age citadel (Troy VI, built c. 1750) is destroyed; Troy VIIa is built soon after.

events.title: Troy VIIa destroyed
events.descr: The city is destroyed around the time of the Late Bronze Age collapse; often discussed as a candidate for Homer's Troy.

events.title: Three-year drought in central Anatolia
events.descr: Tree rings show severe drought in 1198, 1197 and 1196 BCE, suggested as a factor in the Hittite collapse.

events.title: Narmer unifies Egypt
events.descr: Narmer, shown on the Narmer Palette and widely identified with Menes, is credited with conquering Lower Egypt and founding the First Dynasty. His date carries a margin of about 150 years.

events.title: Djoser and the Step Pyramid
events.descr: The first king of the Third Dynasty; his architect Imhotep is credited with the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, the first large stone pyramid.

events.title: Khufu builds the Great Pyramid
events.descr: Khufu's pyramid at Giza, built over about 26 years, stays the tallest structure on Earth for thousands of years. The bar is Khufu's reign; other dating systems put it decades apart.

sources.sourceLocation: Height of the Old Kingdom ('Khufu (2589–2566 BC)')
lead; Historiographical record (table of reign dates)

source.sourceLocation: via Wikipedia: Great Pyramid of Giza (table)
via Wikipedia: Great Pyramid of Giza (table)
'2613–2577 BC' (via Wikipedia: Great Pyramid of Giza)

events.title: Mentuhotep II reunites Egypt
events.descr: The Theban king takes the throne, captures Herakleopolis in his 14th year and completes reunification by his 39th, founding the Middle Kingdom.

sources.sourceLocation: Reunification under the Eleventh Dynasty ('ascended the Theban throne in 2055 BC')

events.title: Senusret III's funerary boat (tree-ring dated)
events.descr: Dendrochronology dates the boat's timber to 1887 ± 11 BCE, an independent check on the conventional reign of Senusret III (1878–1839 BCE).

events.title: Hyksos rule from Avaris (15th Dynasty)
events.descr: Rulers of Levantine origin hold the north of Egypt from Avaris while Theban dynasties rule the south. Scholars' dates for the dynasty differ by a few decades.

events.title: Ahmose I expels the Hyksos
events.descr: After three failed attacks, Ahmose takes Avaris and then Sharuhen after a three-year siege, reuniting Egypt and opening the New Kingdom.

events.title: Reign of Ahmose I
events.descr: Founder of the 18th Dynasty. Published reign dates range over about thirty years; radiocarbon puts his accession at 1570–1544 BCE.

source.sourceLocation: p. 1556 (via Wikipedia: Ahmose I), 95% range 1570–1544 BC

events.title: Egyptian annals mention Tanaju (Danaans?)
events.descr: Messengers from Tanaju appear in Thutmose III's annals, a possible early Egyptian reference to Mycenaean Greeks.

events.title: Reign of Hatshepsut
events.descr: Regent for Thutmose III, then pharaoh in her own right from about her seventh year. She builds at Karnak and Deir el-Bahari and sends a trading expedition to Punt.

events.title: Expedition to Punt
events.descr: In Hatshepsut's ninth year a trading fleet sails to Punt; the voyage is recorded in reliefs at Deir el-Bahari.

events.title: Reign of Thutmose III
events.descr: Co-ruler with Hatshepsut, then sole king and Egypt's great empire-builder in the Levant.

events.title: Battle of Megiddo
events.descr: Thutmose III defeats a Canaanite coalition and besieges Megiddo for seven months: the first battle recorded in reasonably reliable detail.

source.sourceLocation: 'other publications place the battle in 1482 BC or 1479 BC'

events.title: Reign of Akhenaten
events.descr: The pharaoh who promotes the worship of the Aten, changes his name in his fifth year and builds a new capital at Akhetaten (Amarna).

events.title: Amarna period and the Amarna letters
events.descr: Akhetaten is Egypt's capital. Its archive of 382 cuneiform tablets holds letters between the pharaohs and the kings of Babylon, Mitanni, Hatti and Assyria, covering no more than 30 years in the mid-14th century.

events.title: Reign of Tutankhamun
events.descr: The boy king restores the worship of Amun and returns the court to Memphis. His nearly intact tomb (KV62) was found in 1922.

events.title: Reign of Ramesses II
events.descr: A reign of 66 years: Kadesh, the peace with the Hittites, and building from Abu Simbel to the Ramesseum. Most Egyptologists date his accession to 31 May 1279 BCE; older high and middle Egyptian chronologies put it earlier.

source.sourceLocation: 1995, p. 205 (via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings)
1995, p. 205 (via Wikipedia: List of Hittite kings)

events.title: Reign of Merneptah; war with Libyans and Sea Peoples
events.descr: Ramesses II's successor defeats a Libyan invasion joined by groups of Sea Peoples, recorded in the Great Karnak Inscription.

events.title: Battle of the Delta
events.descr: In his eighth year Ramesses III defeats the Sea Peoples at the mouths of the Nile, the best-recorded of their invasions (Medinet Habu).

sources.sourceLocation: lead; infobox; footnotes 1–2 (Drews 2020, p. 51; Beckman 2000, p. 23)

events.title: Shoshenq I founds the 22nd Dynasty
events.descr: A Libyan dynasty takes the throne at Bubastis; Shoshenq campaigns in the Levant.

events.title: Kushite (25th) Dynasty
events.descr: Kings from Kush (Nubia) conquer Egypt, beginning with Piye's march north around 732 BCE, and rule until the Assyrian invasions.

events.title: Assyrian invasions of Egypt
events.descr: Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal defeat the Kushite kings; in 664 BCE the Assyrians sack Thebes and Memphis.

sources.sourceLocation: End of the Third Intermediate Period ('over the period 670–663 BC')

events.title: Assyrians sack Thebes
events.descr: The sack of Egypt's religious capital ends Kushite rule in Egypt.

events.title: Psamtik I reunites Egypt (26th Dynasty)
events.descr: A former Assyrian vassal at Sais, Psamtik (reigned 664–610 BCE) brings Thebes under his rule and Egypt back to independence: the Saite period.

events.title: Battle of Pelusium: Persia conquers Egypt
events.descr: Cambyses II defeats Psamtik III and Egypt becomes a Persian province, beginning the First Achaemenid Period (525–404 BCE).

events.title: First Minoan palaces built
events.descr: The first palaces rise at Knossos, Phaistos and Malia on earlier ceremonial sites; the potter's wheel and Kamares ware appear.

events.title: Linear A in use
events.descr: The undeciphered Minoan script of palace administration and religion, later adapted into Linear B.

events.title: First palaces destroyed
events.descr: Mass destructions, usually blamed on earthquakes, end the Protopalatial period; the palaces are rebuilt larger.

events.title: Shaft graves of Grave Circle A, Mycenae
events.descr: Six rich shaft graves holding 19 bodies, among them the gold 'Mask of Agamemnon'; the cemetery is later enclosed within the citadel.

events.title: Thera (Minoan) eruption
events.descr: A huge eruption buries Akrotiri and sends a tsunami to Crete, late in LM IA. Radiocarbon puts it in the late 17th or 16th century BCE; archaeological synchronisms with Egypt suggest about a century later. The exact year is unsettled.

sources.sourceLocation: prose on high and low chronologies

source.sourceLocation: 1627–1600 BC, olive-tree wiggle-match (via Wikipedia: Minoan eruption)
radiocarbon table: Pearson et al. 2023, 1610–1510 BC (95.4%, IntCal20)

events.title: LM IB destructions across Crete
events.descr: Island-wide destructions, apparently deliberate, end the Neopalatial period; at Knossos the town burns but the palace survives.

sources.sourceLocation: Second Palace period ('partially destroyed around 1450 BC')

events.title: Mycenaeans at Knossos; Linear B appears
events.descr: Knossos becomes a Mycenaean administrative centre keeping its records in Linear B, the earliest written Greek.

events.title: Linear B in use
events.descr: The Mycenaean palace script, deciphered by Michael Ventris in 1952.

events.title: Uluburun shipwreck
events.descr: A merchant ship sinks off southern Anatolia with ten tons of copper, tin, glass and luxury goods: a snapshot of Late Bronze Age trade between Egypt, the Levant, Cyprus and the Aegean.

events.title: Palace of Knossos destroyed
events.descr: A major fire destroys the Mycenaean-era palace; the date is conventional and still debated.

events.title: Lion Gate and citadel walls at Mycenae
events.descr: Mycenae's fortifications are extended to take in Grave Circle A, and the Lion Gate is built.

events.title: Palace of Nestor at Pylos burns
events.descr: The best-preserved Mycenaean palace burns, baking its Linear B archive. Wikipedia's articles give dates from about 1250 to 1180 BCE.

source.sourceLocation: Blegen's dating, end of LH IIIB

events.title: Late Bronze Age collapse
events.descr: Across the eastern Mediterranean, palace economies fail: the Hittite state ends, Mycenaean palaces burn, Ugarit falls, and Egypt fights off the Sea Peoples. Drought, earthquakes, raids and the breakdown of trade are all proposed causes.

events.title: Sub-Mycenaean period
events.descr: The last traces of Mycenaean culture as Greece enters the Iron Age.

events.title: Greek Dark Ages
events.descr: A period of smaller settlements, no writing and little long-distance trade, until the rise of the Greek city-states.

events.title: Neo-Assyrian Empire
events.descr: From the accession of Adad-nirari II, Assyria grows into the largest empire the world had yet seen, ruling from Assur, then Nimrud and Nineveh.

events.title: Sennacherib destroys Babylon
events.descr: After repeated Babylonian revolts, the Assyrian king besieges and destroys the city.

events.title: Nabopolassar crowned king of Babylon
events.descr: Nabopolassar revolts against Assyria, takes Babylon and Nippur and founds the Neo-Babylonian dynasty, allied with the Medes.

sources.sourceLocation: Foundation and the fall of Assyria (Lipschits 2005, pp. 13–14)

events.title: Medes sack Assur
events.descr: The old religious capital of Assyria falls to the Medes.

sources.sourceLocation: Foundation and the fall of Assyria

events.title: Fall of Nineveh
events.descr: Medes and Babylonians besiege Nineveh from May to August; king Sîn-šar-iškun dies and the Assyrian heartland collapses.

sources.sourceLocation: Account of the battle (Lipschits 2005, p. 18; ABC 3)

events.title: Fall of Harran: end of Assyria
events.descr: The last Assyrian king, Ashur-uballit II, is defeated at Harran.

events.title: Reign of Nebuchadnezzar II
events.descr: Babylon's greatest Neo-Babylonian king campaigns across the Levant and rebuilds Babylon on a grand scale.

events.title: Battle of Carchemish
events.descr: The Babylonians under crown prince Nebuchadnezzar defeat Egypt and the last Assyrian forces, taking control of Syria.

events.title: Babylon captures Jerusalem
events.descr: On 2 Adar (16 March 597 BCE) the city falls; King Jeconiah and the court are deported and Zedekiah is installed as a vassal.

events.title: Destruction of Jerusalem and the First Temple
events.descr: After Zedekiah's revolt, Babylon besieges Jerusalem from January 589, then burns the city and the First Temple and deports much of Judah's population.

events.title: Babylonian invasion of Egypt
events.descr: In the fourth year of Amasis, Babylon invades Egypt.

events.title: Cyrus revolts against Astyages
events.descr: Cyrus of Persia overthrows his Median overlord, the beginning of the Achaemenid Empire.

events.title: Reign of Nabonidus
events.descr: The last king of Babylon favours the moon god Sin and spends years in Arabia while his son Belshazzar governs.

events.title: Cyrus takes Babylon
events.descr: After victory at Opis, Persian forces enter Babylon on 12 October 539 BCE; Nabonidus surrenders and the Neo-Babylonian Empire ends.
